specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between density, mass and volume: density = volume mass m ρ = V

primer.text: A feather bag and a metal bag can share a size yet differ wildly in heft. These lessons define density, build the density equation and its triangle, compare materials state by state, and unlock the volume formulae the calculation needs first.

lessons.title: The density equation
sourceHeadings: Formula triangle for density, mass and volume
lessons.opening: Density prices a material: how much mass is packed into each cube of its volume. The equation divides mass by volume, the triangle rearranges it, and the units follow whatever units the two inputs arrive in.
keyPoints: Density is how much mass a material packs into each unit of its volume.
ρ = m ÷ V, with density in kilograms per metre cubed, mass in kilograms and volume in metres cubed.
A formula triangle covering ρ, m or V reproduces every rearrangement of the equation.
Grams with centimetres cubed give grams per centimetre cubed; kilograms with metres cubed give kilograms per metre cubed.

low.restatement: Weigh it, measure the space it fills, divide the first by the second. Hide the symbol you want on the triangle and the other two show you whether to multiply or divide.
low.analogy: A crowd count: people (mass) spread through a hall (volume) — a cramped hall has a dense crowd, an empty one does not.
low.examPointer: State the unit with the answer and match it to the input units — mixing grams with metres cubed is the classic unit slip.

medium.restatement: The density equation ρ = m/V divides the mass of a sample by the volume it occupies, so equal masses in smaller volumes are denser. The unit follows the inputs: grams and centimetres cubed yield grams per centimetre cubed, kilograms and metres cubed yield kilograms per metre cubed, and the triangle encodes all three rearrangements.
medium.analogy: A population density map: the same city spread over a larger county reads as a lower figure — area here plays volume's role.
medium.examPointer: Convert lengths to metres and masses to kilograms before dividing whenever the question wants kg/m³ — quote the unit to bank the mark.

check.stem: Which equation defines density?

options.text: density = mass ÷ volume
options.explanation: Mass divided by the volume it fills.

options.text: density = volume ÷ mass
options.explanation: That inverts the relationship.

options.text: density = mass × volume
options.explanation: Multiplying has no physical meaning here.

options.text: density = weight ÷ area
options.explanation: That is pressure's territory.

check.stem: A material's mass is measured in kilograms and its volume in metres cubed. Its density unit is

options.text: kilograms per metre cubed
options.explanation: The unit follows the input units directly.

options.text: grams per centimetre cubed
options.explanation: That pair belongs to gram-and-centimetre inputs.

options.text: newtons per kilogram
options.explanation: That is gravitational field strength.

options.text: metres cubed per kilogram
options.explanation: That inverts the unit.

check.stem: Two identical bags hold the same volume, one filled with feathers and one with metal. What can be said about their masses?

options.text: the metal bag has much the greater mass in the same volume, so the higher density
options.explanation: Equal volumes: the heavier filling is the denser material.

options.text: the feather bag is denser because feathers pile tightly
options.explanation: Feathers pack far more air between fibres.

options.text: both bags have the same density because their volumes match
options.explanation: Equal volume with different mass means different density.

options.text: neither bag has a measurable density
options.explanation: Both are perfectly measurable.

check.stem: Why does a gas have a lower density than the same substance as a solid?

options.text: its particles are spread out, so the same mass occupies a larger volume
options.explanation: Same mass over more volume divides to a smaller density.

options.text: gas particles weigh less than solid particles
options.explanation: The particles are identical; only their spacing changes.

options.text: gases have no mass at all
options.explanation: Gases are massy, just spread thin.

options.text: solid particles are always larger
options.explanation: Particle size does not change with state.

check.stem: On the density formula triangle, covering V leaves

options.text: m over ρ, so V = m ÷ ρ
options.explanation: Hiding the volume exposes the mass over the density.

options.text: ρ over m, so V = ρ ÷ m
options.explanation: That inverts the rearrangement.

options.text: ρ × m, so V = ρ × m
options.explanation: That would multiply, not divide.

options.text: nothing useful — the triangle only finds density
options.explanation: The triangle serves all three rearrangements.

check.stem: State the density equation in symbols and name each quantity with its unit.
check.modelAnswer: ρ = m ÷ V, where ρ is the density in kilograms per metre cubed, m is the mass in kilograms and V is the volume in metres cubed.

check.stem: State what the density of a material tells you about its mass and volume.
check.modelAnswer: The density tells you how much mass is packed into each unit of the material's volume.

check.stem: Explain why a balloon can occupy more space than a small lead bar yet contain far less mass.
check.modelAnswer: Density divides mass by volume, and the balloon's filling — mostly gas — spreads very little mass through a large volume, while the lead bars cram a large mass into a small one. Occupied space alone decides nothing; the mass-per-volume ratio decides everything.

check.stem: A cube measures 2 m along each edge and has a mass of 1600 kg. Calculate its density.

lessons.title: Density across states and materials
sourceHeadings: Comparing the density of solids and gases
lessons.opening: The same substance changes its density with its state: packed particles make dense solids and liquids, while spread-out particles thin gases out. Material choice matters just as much — equal sizes, wildly different hefts.
keyPoints: Objects made from low-density materials carry low masses; equal-sized objects of high-density materials carry high masses.
A bag of feathers is far lighter than the same bag filled with metal.
Gases are generally less dense than solids because their particles sit far apart.
The same substance is denser in solid or liquid form than as a gas.

low.restatement: Squeeze the same atoms closer together and the density climbs: solid tight, liquid close, gas sparse. Swap the material instead and the atom's own heft sets the scale — feathers float, lead sinks.
low.analogy: Three classrooms: packed full (solid), half full (liquid), one pupil per corridor (gas) — same school, very different crowding.
low.examPointer: Comparisons must fix everything but one variable — equal volumes for material comparisons, equal substance for state comparisons.

medium.restatement: Density tracks particle spacing: a substance's solid and liquid states pack particles closely, so both out-dense the gas state where the same mass disperses through far more volume. Across materials at equal volume, the heavier-particle, tighter-packed material wins the density contest outright.
medium.analogy: Packing for three trips: folded tight (solid), loosely rolled (liquid), scattered across the whole suitcase (gas) — same belongings, three bulks.
medium.examPointer: When a question compares states, answer with particle spacing and the mass-over-volume consequence, not with 'gases are light', which explains nothing.

check.stem: Equal-sized blocks of wood and lead: which has the greater mass?

options.text: the lead block, because lead is the denser material
options.explanation: Equal volumes make the density ranking decide the masses.

options.text: the wooden block, because wood is heavier grain by grain
options.explanation: Wood is the less dense material.

options.text: neither — equal sizes mean equal masses
options.explanation: Equal size does not equalise different materials.

options.text: whichever block was made first
options.explanation: History sets no mass.

check.stem: Water becomes steam. What happens to the density of the water you are watching?

options.text: it drops sharply, because the same mass now spreads through much more volume
options.explanation: Evaporation inflates the volume at constant mass.

options.text: it rises, because steam is hotter
options.explanation: Temperature alone does not set the density jump here.

options.text: it stays the same — states never change density
options.explanation: State changes rearrange particle spacing dramatically.

options.text: it doubles, because steam particles split
options.explanation: Particles do not split on boiling.

check.stem: Which statement about the three states of one substance is correct?

options.text: solid and liquid are both denser than the gas state
options.explanation: The gas spreads the same mass over more volume.

options.text: the gas is denser than the liquid
options.explanation: The ordering is reversed.

options.text: all three states share one density
options.explanation: Spacing changes with state, so density does too.

options.text: only the solid has any density at all
options.explanation: Every state has a measurable density.

check.stem: A workshop sorts offcuts by mass alone to guess density. What must it also know?

options.text: each offcut's volume, because density compares mass to volume
options.explanation: Mass without volume prices nothing.

options.text: the offcuts' colours
options.explanation: Colour carries no density information.

options.text: the workshop's temperature only
options.explanation: Temperature is not the missing quantity here.

options.text: nothing else — mass alone fixes density
options.explanation: Density is a ratio, not a raw mass.

check.stem: Which comparison is a fair density comparison?

options.text: the same substance as solid versus as gas
options.explanation: One variable — the state — changes.

options.text: a balloon of helium against a bar of lead of any size
options.explanation: Both material and volume differ at once.

options.text: a warm feather against a cold anvil
options.explanation: Material, size and temperature all differ.

options.text: a full gas jar against an empty one
options.explanation: One side has no sample to compare.

check.stem: State why gases are generally less dense than solids.
check.modelAnswer: Gas particles are more spread out, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and the mass-per-volume ratio falls.

check.stem: State which fills a same-size bag to a greater mass: feathers or metal.
check.modelAnswer: Metal fills the same-size bag to a far greater mass, because it is the denser material.

check.stem: Explain why comparing the densities of two different materials is fairest when their volumes match.
check.modelAnswer: Density is the ratio of mass to volume, so a fair material comparison holds the volume fixed and lets only the material differ. With volumes equal, the material with the greater mass is unambiguously the denser one.

check.stem: A State changes from liquid to solid and its volume shrinks slightly while its mass stays constant. State what happens to its density.
check.modelAnswer: The density increases, because the same mass now divides by a smaller volume.

lessons.title: Finding volume first
sourceHeadings: Calculating volume to help obtain density values
Common formulae required to calculate the volumes of objects to then obtain their density
lessons.opening: Density questions often hide the volume inside the object's shape. Out come the geometry formulae — cubes, cuboids, cylinders and spheres — and only after the volume is rebuilt can the density equation divide.
keyPoints: An object's volume is not always stated and must be calculated from its shape first.
Each regular shape carries its own volume formula — cube, cuboid, cylinder and sphere among them.
Once the volume is known, the density equation divides mass by volume as usual.
Lengths must enter the volume formulae in metres so the density lands in kilograms per metre cubed.

low.restatement: Measure the edges, apply the shape's own formula, then divide the mass by what you get. The geometry is the servant: it exists to feed the density equation a volume.
low.analogy: A recipe: the shape's formula is the measuring jug step — only after pouring the volume can you cook the density.
low.examPointer: Write the volume formula explicitly before substituting — examiners award the method mark even where arithmetic slips.

medium.restatement: Volume reconstruction precedes density calculation whenever the volume is not given directly: the object's shape selects the formula, the lengths are multiplied through in metres, and the resulting volume in metres cubed feeds ρ = m/V. Errors in the geometry propagate straight into the density, which is why the formula must be stated.
medium.analogy: A two-stage rocket: the geometry stage lifts off first, and only its burnout hands the mass-over-volume stage its payload.
medium.examPointer: State the shape formula, convert lengths to metres, then divide — and carry the units through the volume step, not just the final answer.

check.stem: Why might a density calculation need a volume formula first?

options.text: the object's volume is often not stated and must come from its shape
options.explanation: Geometry supplies the missing input.

options.text: mass can only be found from volume formulas
options.explanation: Mass comes from the balance.

options.text: density formulas require geometry by definition
options.explanation: The density equation needs only a volume value, however obtained.

options.text: volumes are always too small to measure
options.explanation: They are measurable; the question is what is given.

check.stem: Which volume belongs to a cuboid of edges 2 m, 3 m and 4 m?

options.text: 24 m³
options.explanation: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 cubic metres.

options.text: 9 m³
options.explanation: That adds the edges instead of multiplying.

options.text: 24 m²
options.explanation: Volume carries cubic units.

options.text: 12 m³
options.explanation: That drops one edge.

check.stem: An object's edges were measured in centimetres. What must happen before the volume feeds a kg/m³ density?

options.text: the lengths convert to metres, giving a volume in metres cubed
options.explanation: Unit discipline decides the density's unit.

options.text: nothing — centimetres feed kg/m³ directly
options.explanation: Mixed units corrupt the answer.

options.text: the mass converts to grams instead
options.explanation: The target unit is kilograms per metre cubed.

options.text: the volume converts to litres
options.explanation: Litres are not the target volume unit here.

check.stem: A cylinder's radius and height are known. What is the shape-formula step for its volume?

options.text: multiply π by the radius squared by the height
options.explanation: V = πr²h for a cylinder.

options.text: multiply the radius by the height
options.explanation: That misses π and the square.

options.text: cube the radius
options.explanation: Cubing suits cubes, not cylinders.

options.text: add the radius to the height
options.explanation: Adding never builds a volume.

check.stem: A slab measures 0.02 m × 0.4 m × 0.9 m and has a mass of 60 kg. Which working finds its density?

options.text: volume 0.0072 m³, then 60 ÷ 0.0072 ≈ 8300 kg/m³
options.explanation: The geometry feeds the division; the answer rounds to 2 s.f.
That inverts the division.

options.text: volume 1.32 m³, then 60 ÷ 1.32 ≈ 45 kg/m³
options.explanation: That adds the dimensions instead of multiplying.

options.text: density 60 × 0.0072 ≈ 0.43 kg/m³
options.explanation: Multiplying never divides mass by volume.

check.stem: State the volume formula for a cube of edge length L.
check.modelAnswer: The volume of a cube is L × L × L, the edge length cubed.

check.stem: State what must be calculated before the density equation when the volume is not given.
check.modelAnswer: The object's volume must be calculated from its shape using the appropriate formula first.

check.stem: Explain why an error in the volume step propagates straight into the final density.
check.modelAnswer: The density divides the mass by the calculated volume, so the volume sits in the denominator of the final step. Any volume error — a wrong formula, unconverted units — rescales the density directly, which is why the geometry must be written and checked before dividing.

check.stem: A sphere of radius 0.1 m has a mass of 4.2 kg. Taking the sphere volume as 4 ÷ 3 × π × r³ and π ≈ 3, calculate its density.

glossary.definition: How much mass a material packs into each unit of its volume.
The density unit that follows when mass is in kilograms and volume in metres cubed.
The amount of three-dimensional space an object occupies, in metres cubed here.

workedExample.prompt: A paving slab has a mass of 73 kg and dimensions 0.04 m × 0.5 m × 0.85 m. Calculate the density, in kg/m³, of the material from which the paving slab is made.
steps: List the known quantities: mass m = 73 kg, edges 0.04 m, 0.5 m and 0.85 m.
State the density equation: ρ = m ÷ V.
Round to two significant figures: ρ = 4300 kg/m³.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The density of the slab material is about 4300 kg/m³.
